skills.name: benchmarking
skills.description: Guide for building, running, and analyzing Nanvix performance benchmarks. Use this when asked about benchmark setup, execution, or interpretation.

skills.name: build
skills.description: Guide for building, formatting, linting, and spell-checking Nanvix with z. Use this when asked to build or validate the repository.

skills.name: ci-cd-pipeline
skills.description: Guide for Nanvix CI and GitHub Actions workflow behavior, including local pipeline execution and matrix coverage. Use this when asked about CI checks, workflow failures, or release flow.

skills.name: coding-standards
skills.description: Detailed Nanvix coding, documentation, and review standards across Rust, C/C++, Python, and Shell. Use this when asked to implement or review code quality conventions.

skills.name: daemon-development
skills.description: Guide for developing and debugging Nanvix daemons, including guest daemons and host linuxd behavior. Use this when asked about daemon architecture or daemon changes.

skills.name: gdb-debugging
skills.description: Guide for debugging Nanvix guests using GDB remote debugging over the microvm machine type. Use this when asked about attaching GDB, setting breakpoints, or stepping through kernel code.

skills.name: kernel-development
skills.description: Guide for modifying and debugging the Nanvix kernel architecture and kernel-call paths. Use this when asked about kernel internals or kernel implementation changes.

skills.name: library-development
skills.description: Guide for creating and modifying Nanvix libraries under src/libs, including guest no_std and host std crates. Use this when asked about library architecture or crate changes.

skills.name: test
skills.description: Guide for running Nanvix tests with z. Use this when asked to run unit tests, integration tests, or the full test suite.

skills.name: test-development
skills.description: Guide for writing, running, and debugging Nanvix unit, integration, and system tests in Rust and C/C++. Use this when asked about test implementation or failures.

skills.name: troubleshooting
skills.description: Guide for diagnosing Nanvix build, runtime, and test failures, including cleanup and debugging workflows. Use this when asked to investigate errors or unstable behavior.

skills.name: user-app-development
skills.description: Guide for developing, building, and running Nanvix user-space applications across supported runtimes and languages. Use this when asked about guest app implementation or execution.

skills.name: pptx
skills.description: Use this skill any time a .pptx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates, layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.

skills.name: ast-consistency
skills.description: AST-level exec fidelity checking tools and pre-approved deviations. Use after modifying source files to verify exec code is unchanged.

skills.name: body-removal
skills.description: Remove function bodies from Rust/Verus source files to produce signature-only views. Used before the view-design phase to prevent implementation anchoring.

skills.name: bug-reporting
skills.description: Classify and report bugs found during Verus verification. Distinguishes true bugs from missing constraints and verifier limitations. Use when a verification failure might indicate a code bug.

skills.name: caller-analysis
skills.description: Analyze callers of a Rust module to understand usage expectations for Verus verification. Produces a caller-perspective analysis covering all functions with their visibility and call relationships.

skills.name: crate-analysis
skills.description: Principles for verification order in multi-file Rust crates. Verify top-level modules first (top-down), writing dependency specs on demand as verification drills down. The pipeline tool handles ordering automatically.

skills.name: proof-extraction
skills.description: Extract large inline proof blocks from exec code into named lemmas in .proof.rs. Use when polishing verified code to improve readability and proof organization.

skills.name: proof-minimization
skills.description: Remove redundant proof artifacts (assertions, lemmas, hints, dead code) without weakening guarantees. Use when polishing verified code to reduce verbosity.

skills.name: property-analysis
skills.description: How to analyze source code and identify verification properties — the WHAT of verification. Covers module understanding, property discovery across four dimensions (functional correctness, safety, liveness, structural consistency), and quality review. Use this skill when deciding what to verify for a new module, writing property_analysis.md, or updating global_properties.md.

skills.name: proving-guide
skills.description: Proving methodology and mindset for Verus verification: function-by-function approach, persistence through failures, clean verification, and bug reporting. Use when writing proofs or resolving verification failures.

skills.name: review-methodology
skills.description: Reviewer mental model: independent, skeptical, hands-on, strict. Applies to all pipeline phases.

skills.name: spec-completeness
skills.description: Detect specification incompleteness via nondeterminism checking. Given a Verus function spec, automatically determine whether the spec uniquely determines the output for each valid input. If not, use type-guided binary search to construct a concrete witness (input + two valid but different outputs). No LLM needed — pure SMT-based.

skills.name: spec-design
skills.description: How to write good Verus specs. Covers spec quality principles (anti-patterns, error paths), spec classification (internal, external-top, external-bottom trust boundaries), View abstraction design, and static vs dynamic enforcement. Use when writing or reviewing Verus specs.

skills.name: spec-drift-check
skills.description: Detect spec weakening via tree-sitter comparison against a baseline SHA. Use in specification, proving, and cheating-elimination phases to enforce that requires/ensures are never silently removed or relaxed.

skills.name: tcb-plan
skills.description: Phase 0 of the verus-ai pipeline: classify every callee from user-provided entry points into 8 trust verdicts using probe (Cat-A hard-reject) + catalog (Cat-B silent-model) + AI residue, then produce a frozen approved-trust-boundaries.json that downstream phases honor as a hard whitelist. Use when starting a new project to pre-authorize all trust decisions before any verification work.

skills.name: verification-order
skills.description: Determine function-level verification order within a module using the verification plan. Use at the start of proving to know which function to verify first and how to sequence work.

skills.name: verus-constraints
skills.description: Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code.

skills.name: verus-setup
skills.description: Set up Verus formal verification infrastructure for a Rust project. Covers workspace-level config (vstd dependency, cfg flags, version pinning, Makefile, scripts) and per-crate config (metadata, cfg-gated includes, spec/proof stubs). Use this skill when preparing a repo or crate for Verus verification, adding make verify support, or integrating cheating detection into a build.

skills.name: verus-syntax
skills.description: Verus attribute-based syntax reference for exec functions. Covers #[verus_spec], #[verus_verify], proof!{}, proof_decl!{}, loop invariants. See GUIDE.md for advanced patterns, syntax_attr.rs for the official example.

skills.name: view-design
skills.description: How to design a View type that represents abstract state from the caller's perspective. Input: caller analysis + property concepts. Must NOT see implementation code.

skills.name: customize-cloud-agent
skills.description: Skill for customizing the Copilot cloud agent (formerly known as Copilot coding agent) environment, including copilot-setup-steps.yml configuration, preinstalling tools and dependencies, runners, and settings. Use when the user mentions copilot-setup-steps, copilot setup steps, or wants to configure the cloud agent environment.

4. //! # Sparse Bitmap

---
name: proof-extraction
description: "Extract large inline proof blocks from exec code into named lemmas in .proof.rs. Use when polishing verified code to improve readability and proof organization."
---

# Proof Extraction

Extract large inline `proof { ... }` blocks from exec code into named lemmas
in the proof file (`<module>.proof.rs`).

## Why

Large inline proof blocks hurt readability and make exec code hard to review.
Extracting them into lemmas with clear names documents *what* is being proven
and makes proofs reusable.

## Tool

Use `check_proof_blocks` (MCP tool) or the CLI script to find blocks:

```bash
python3 scripts/check_proof_blocks.py <source_file> --threshold 5 --all
```

Output shows each proof block with its enclosing function, line range, and size.
Blocks marked `⚠️ EXTRACT` exceed the threshold.

## Rules

| Block size  | Action |
|-------------|--------|
| >5 lines    | **Must** extract into a lemma in `.proof.rs` |
| 4-5 lines   | Extract if generic/reusable; keep if tightly coupled to exec context |
| 1-3 lines   | Keep inline |

## Extraction Process

For each block to extract:

1. Read the proof block and identify what it proves (the key `assert` / property).
2. Create `proof fn lemma_<descriptive_name>` in `.proof.rs` with:
   - `requires`: the preconditions the proof depends on
   - `ensures`: the property being proven (must be strong enough for the call site)
3. Replace the inline block with a 1-3 line lemma call.
4. Run verification to confirm it still passes.

## Loop Invariants

Long loop invariants (>5 clauses) also hurt readability. Factor out groups
of related clauses into named `spec fn` predicates:

```rust
// Before: 10 invariant clauses inline
while i < n
    invariant
        0 <= i <= n,
        result.len() == i,
        forall|j: int| 0 <= j < i ==> result[j] == f(input[j]),
        ... // 7 more clauses
{ ... }

// After: grouped into named predicates
spec fn loop_partial_result_ok(result: Seq<T>, input: Seq<T>, i: int) -> bool {
    result.len() == i
    && forall|j: int| 0 <= j < i ==> result[j] == f(input[j])
}

while i < n
    invariant
        0 <= i <= n,
        loop_partial_result_ok(result@, input@, i as int),
        ... // remaining clauses
{ ... }
```

Keep trivial bounds (`0 <= i <= n`) inline. Extract semantic groups
(data consistency, structural invariants) into named predicates.

## Naming

Lemma names describe what they prove:
- ✅ `lemma_set_bit_preserves_inv`
- ✅ `lemma_alloc_range_bounded`
- ❌ `lemma_proof_block_1`
- ❌ `lemma_helper`

## Constraints

- Do NOT change exec logic.
- Do NOT change spec function signatures.
- Verification must still pass after extraction.

data.content:
Your plan is mostly sound, but I see a few important blind spots.

## Blocking Issues

### 1. Some “keep inline” blocks still violate the stated >5-line extraction rule
**Impact:** If `check_proof_blocks.py --threshold 5` remains the acceptance criterion, blocks of 6–8 lines will still fail the polish task even if they are “just lemma calls.”  
**Examples:** `sort_chunks_by_offset:509-516`, `commit_cross_chunk_alloc:761-767`, `796-801`, gap/set-bit cases, `alloc_range:1512-1517`.  
**Recommended fix:** Either extract every block reported by the checker, or confirm the checker ignores “simple lemma-call-only” blocks. Otherwise these need tiny wrapper lemmas too, even if mechanically boring.

### 2. `try_alloc_cross_chunk_from` pfp update block contains a ghost mutation
You called out the ghost mutation in block #4, but block #6 also mutates ghost state:

```rust
let ghost old_pfp = phase1b_free_prefixes;
phase1b_free_prefixes = phase1b_free_prefixes.push(take as int);
```

**Impact:** A proof lemma cannot perform this mutation on the caller’s ghost variable, so extracting the whole 28-line block as `lemma_pfp_update_after_check_walk` will not work directly.  
**Recommended fix:** Split it like block #4:

```rust
proof {
    let ghost old_pfp = phase1b_free_prefixes;
    phase1b_free_prefixes = phase1b_free_prefixes.push(take as int);
    lemma_pfp_update_after_check_walk(... old_pfp, phase1b_free_prefixes, ...);
}
```

The lemma should prove the post-push properties, not perform the push.

## Non-Blocking Issues

### 3. Be careful with `old(self)` in extracted lemmas
Passing `old_self_view` is the right direction, but extracted lemmas cannot magically prove facts like:

```rust
old_chunks_seq =~= old(self).chunks@
```

unless that relationship is already a `requires`.

**Impact:** You may end up with lemmas whose ensures are only provable because the caller already knows the same fact, making them brittle or circular.  
**Recommended fix:** For any lemma needing `old(self)`, pass only ghost/spec values such as `old_self_view: SparseBitmapView` or `old_self_chunks: Seq<Chunk>`, and make relationships explicit in `requires`. Keep call-site assertions for facts that are uniquely tied to `old(self)` if extraction makes the lemma unnatural.

### 4. The 51-line block split point looks right, but the second lemma may be too small
Splitting around:

```rust
committed = committed + take as int;
```

is necessary. But lines 1073–1081 are only a conditional arithmetic/chain-position proof.

**Impact:** Extracting that tail may create an awkward lemma with many parameters for little readability gain.  
**Recommended fix:** Extract the pre-mutation part. Then either keep the 1073–1081 tail inline if it drops under the checker threshold, or combine it into a lemma specifically about “next chunk offset after consuming remaining” with minimal params.

### 5. Minimization could destabilize triggers
Your concern is valid. Several “redundant” assertions are likely trigger material, especially assertions involving:

- `#[trigger] old_chunks_seq[(i + 1) as int]`
- `self.chunks@[k]`
- `phase1b_free_prefixes[i]`
- extensional equality `=~=`

**Impact:** Removing them may not change the logical proof but may break SMT instantiation.  
**Recommended fix:** Minimize only after extraction verifies cleanly. Remove assertions one small batch at a time, grouped by proof block/function, and revert quickly if failures are quantifier-trigger-related.

## Suggestions

### 6. Prefer lemmas with semantic postconditions, not “bundle of local asserts”
For extracted lemmas, avoid ensuring every intermediate assertion. Ensure only what the call site/loop invariant needs, e.g.:

- structure preserved after chunk update
- lifted set bits equals old lifted set bits union range
- remaining equals relevant `seq_sum_from`
- next offset matches expected global position

This keeps the proof file useful rather than just relocating inline clutter.

### 7. Re-run the proof-block checker after extraction, not just Verus
Verification passing is necessary but not sufficient for this polish task. The checker is the metric that identified the problem.

Overall: the plan is good, but fix the ghost-mutation issue in the pfp block and don’t leave >5-line inline blocks unless the checker/task explicitly permits them.

# Proof Extraction

Extract large inline `proof { ... }` blocks from exec code into named lemmas
in the proof file (`<module>.proof.rs`).

## Why

Large inline proof blocks hurt readability and make exec code hard to review.
Extracting them into lemmas with clear names documents *what* is being proven
and makes proofs reusable.

## Tool

Use `check_proof_blocks` (MCP tool) or the CLI script to find blocks:

```bash
python3 scripts/check_proof_blocks.py <source_file> --threshold 5 --all
```

Output shows each proof block with its enclosing function, line range, and size.
Blocks marked `⚠️ EXTRACT` exceed the threshold.

## Rules

| Block size  | Action |
|-------------|--------|
| >5 lines    | **Must** extract into a lemma in `.proof.rs` |
| 4-5 lines   | Extract if generic/reusable; keep if tightly coupled to exec context |
| 1-3 lines   | Keep inline |

## Extraction Process

For each block to extract:

1. Read the proof block and identify what it proves (the key `assert` / property).
2. Create `proof fn lemma_<descriptive_name>` in `.proof.rs` with:
   - `requires`: the preconditions the proof depends on
   - `ensures`: the property being proven (must be strong enough for the call site)
3. Replace the inline block with a 1-3 line lemma call.
4. Run verification to confirm it still passes.

## Loop Invariants

Long loop invariants (>5 clauses) also hurt readability. Factor out groups
of related clauses into named `spec fn` predicates:

```rust
// Before: 10 invariant clauses inline
while i < n
    invariant
        0 <= i <= n,
        result.len() == i,
        forall|j: int| 0 <= j < i ==> result[j] == f(input[j]),
        ... // 7 more clauses
{ ... }

// After: grouped into named predicates
spec fn loop_partial_result_ok(result: Seq<T>, input: Seq<T>, i: int) -> bool {
    result.len() == i
    && forall|j: int| 0 <= j < i ==> result[j] == f(input[j])
}

while i < n
    invariant
        0 <= i <= n,
        loop_partial_result_ok(result@, input@, i as int),
        ... // remaining clauses
{ ... }
```

Keep trivial bounds (`0 <= i <= n`) inline. Extract semantic groups
(data consistency, structural invariants) into named predicates.

## Naming

Lemma names describe what they prove:
- ✅ `lemma_set_bit_preserves_inv`
- ✅ `lemma_alloc_range_bounded`
- ❌ `lemma_proof_block_1`
- ❌ `lemma_helper`

## Constraints

- Do NOT change exec logic.
- Do NOT change spec function signatures.
- Verification must still pass after extraction.
